column2: The Jerry Wolpert affair: an offer withdrawn, anger, death

Wolpert, a former student reputed to be very gifted, believes after a visit that he has received a firm offer, resigns from his job, then receives a letter from Natasha explaining that the reorganization makes any offer impossible; he writes an incendiary letter denouncing a disgusting double-dealing and a fraudulent college; Natasha speaks of a misunderstanding (individuals' wishes taken for a Board decision)

An exhibition of ten artist couples, including Pollock and Krasner. Elaine shows her wide-eyed Self Portrait (around 1942); Bill's canvas is not identified. Stuart Preston (New York Times) judges that on the whole the husbands are bolder and accuses the wives of taking only the design or color of their husbands' styles, citing the de Koonings and the Pollocks; ARTnews echoes him.
The club is founded by eighteen members, including de Kooning, Kline, and Reinhardt, in a loft at 39 East Eighth Street; it becomes simply “The Club.”

The New Yorkers found the Club. De Kooning: they wanted a loft rather than staying in those damned cafeterias; the Greeks and the Italians each have their social clubs along Eighth Avenue; they wanted nothing to do with art — just a place to go at night, drink coffee, have a few drinks, talk.

Anni Albers becomes the first textile artist to have a solo exhibition at MoMA, but cannot persuade the museum to buy her only surviving Bauhaus tapestry.
A solo exhibition; for it she creates a series of hanging screens in leno weave to produce a material that lets light through.

Rauschenberg studies with Albers at Black Mountain

During his first year (six months are mentioned), Rauschenberg takes Albers's drawing and watercolor classes, so intimidated that his only aim becomes to please him. Albers tells him that he cannot draw, that his whole childhood has been wasted; he finds him too sloppy for collage and too heavy-handed in drawing. Albers likes open spaces and fine lines, “the Matisse kind of thing.”
He leaves Black Mountain in summer 1949, launched in the radical direction of his monochrome exercises; he feels less of a hick than when he arrived from Paris.
Study at the Art Students League
He studies at the Art Students League with Morris Kantor and Vaclav Vytlacil; his best work is done at home, first in a rented studio, then in a space on Willett Street without heat or water.
A woodcut whose block is progressively cut with lines, the image emerging from black to white in fourteen stages; one of the few works of this period along with his photographs.

Resignations in solidarity with Dreier
In protest against the treatment of Dreier, the Alberses, Trude Guermonprez, and Charlotte Schlesinger resign; shortly afterward, Gropius resigns from the advisory council.
The January 1949 crisis and a cascade of resignations

After the January 1949 crisis, when Pittenger agrees to guide the college through a transition period, the Alberses, Schlesinger, and Guermonprez make their resignations public, joined by Dreier. Albers agrees to teach until the end of the semester.
Josef Albers resigns and the rectorship is offered to Fuller
In spring 1949, Josef Albers resigns; Fuller's electrifying presence, notably his role as Baron Medusa, earns him the offer of the college's vacant rectorship. He declines.

After the success of the second assembly of the geodesic dome at Black Mountain, Fuller promotes it as a 'design revolution' to journalists, military strategists, and students: light and portable, transportable by air to inaccessible sites, cheap thanks to aluminum (airplane hangars).

The lecture “A Desperate View” and The Club
De Kooning's lecture “A Desperate View”

Bill delivers his now famous lecture there: art comes from his feeling of desperation; order can only come from above, and order for him means being ordered about, and so a limitation; style is a fraud, wanting to give oneself a style is an excuse for anxiety; the subject of art is space, which the artist fills with an “attitude” that never comes from him alone; one belongs to a group or movement because one cannot help it. Few know that Elaine largely prepared the text: Bill talked, she took notes, they went over the text again and again, she made suggestions, days and days of work.

De Kooning delivers “A Desperate View,” steeped in Kierkegaard's Fear and Trembling: his interest in desperation lies only in the fact that he sometimes finds himself desperate; in Genesis, in the beginning was the void and God acted upon it; for an artist that is clear enough; one is forever utterly lost in space — one can float in it, fly in it, hang in it, and today trembling in it seems best, or at any rate very fashionable.

Leaving for New Haven and Yale

Toward the end of 1950, the Alberses move to New Haven, where Josef takes up a post as chairman of the Department of Design at the Yale University School of the Fine Arts; he will live in Connecticut for twenty-five years and die there in 1976, at eighty-eight

Albers accepts a year at Harvard (the brick wall America for Gropius's complex at the Harvard Law School) and in 1950, at 62, begins his long association with Yale and the Homage to the Square series.

Albers chairman of the design department at Yale

Albers headed Yale's design department for most of the 1950s; yet he saw himself as a rebel, the victim of power-hungry professors and their supporters within the very institution he had spent his life defying.
Albers accepts the chairmanship of Yale's Department of Design

From Cambridge, where he teaches at the Graduate School of Design, Albers writes to Perdekamp: in August he will go to New Haven, having accepted a position at Yale as chairman of the Department of Design (formerly the Department of Painting and Sculpture).

The Alberses' work at the Harvard Graduate Center

Both Alberses work with Gropius on the Harvard Graduate Center: Josef designs a brick fireplace wall for a common room, its subtle abstract pattern obtained by the varying angles of the white bricks in the mortar; Anni creates woven partitions and bedspreads with bold abstract patterns.
Clement Greenberg teaches at Black Mountain

A critic recommended to the college by de Kooning, Greenberg teaches there in 1950; he credits the students with an impressive intensity but concludes that not much came of it as art, only a few famous names.
